ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All experiments were done in agreement with the local ethics committee from the University of Iceland and the Declaration of Helsinki.
All experiments were done in agreement with the local ethics committee from the University of Iceland and the Declaration of Helsinki.

Another study conducted by Alvarez and Oliva (2009) provided further evidence in favor of the attentionindependent nature of ensemble perception: While participants were attending and tracking a set of moving dots, they were still reliably able to detect orientation changes of an ensemble of Gabors in the unattended background.
table.formatted: Another study conducted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Alvarez and Oliva (2009)</ref> provided further evidence in favor of the attentionindependent nature of ensemble perception: While participants were attending and tracking a set of moving dots, they were still reliably able to detect orientation changes of an ensemble of Gabors in the unattended background.

table.text: They found that unattended ensembles affected performance only when their summary statistics matched the target category that the participants were searching for.
In Experiment 1, the participants were asked to look for the smallest or largest circle, thereby making size task relevant.
Before search, participants were given a visual cue that constituted the target template and the similarity between the cue and the target to be presented during search was manipulated.

Material & Methods Participants 25 observers participated in the experiment. 17 participants were undergraduates (17 females; M = 25.5 years, SD = 5.99, 8 males; M = 27.8 years, SD = 6.08) from the University of Iceland who participated in this experiment for course credit and 8 staff members from the University of Iceland participated the experiment for gift card (3000 isk).

table.text: All participants provided written informed consent and were tested for colorblindness with Ishihara's test for color deficiency (Ishihara, 2004) before the experiment.
table.formatted: All participants provided written informed consent and were tested for colorblindness with Ishihara's test for color deficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Ishihara, 2004)</ref> before the experiment.

table.text: Participants were seated 57 cm away from a 24-inch monitor (ASUS, VX248h, resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels; refresh rate: 60 Hz).
Participants were instructed to find the odd-colored target and report the location of the black dot (left or right) using the corresponding arrow keys (left/right arrow) on the keyboard.
In the proceeding ensemble trial, participants were instructed to estimate the average orientation of the entire ensemble.

Perceptual biases were found in the experiment showing that orientation judgements of the participants were biased towards the target color or away from the distractor color, in other words, the encoded attentional templates formed during the search task affected observers' ensemble estimates.
In the Distractor Repeat and the Target Repeat condition both templates were active, but participants were only biased by the templates color which matched one of the subsets.
However, in the Both Repeat condition participants were biased by both templates at the same time.
All participants provided written informed consent and were tested for colorblindness with Ishihara's test for color deficiency (Ishihara, 2004) before the experiment.
table.formatted: All participants provided written informed consent and were tested for colorblindness with Ishihara's test for color deficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Ishihara, 2004)</ref> before the experiment.

table.text: Participants were seated 57 cm away from a 24-inch monitor (ASUS, VX248h, resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels; refresh rate: 60 Hz).
On each block, participants completed an ensemble task which was preceded by 4-5 visual searches with identical target and distractor colors.
Participants were asked to report the size of the target circle from the memorized array of colored circles.

Importantly, their findings indicated that when participants were asked to report the size of an individual item rather than an ensemble average, task-relevant color grouping affected the representation of individual items.
Our task required attentional selection guided by the color, and participants were expected to estimate average mean orientation of the lines.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Another study conducted by Alvarez and Oliva (2009) provided further evidence in favor of the attentionindependent nature of ensemble perception: While participants were attending and tracking a set of moving dots, they were still reliably able to detect orientation changes of an ensemble of Gabors in the unattended background.

> They found that unattended ensembles affected performance only when their summary statistics matched the target category that the participants were searching for.

> In Experiment 1, the participants were asked to look for the smallest or largest circle, thereby making size task relevant.

> Before search, participants were given a visual cue that constituted the target template and the similarity between the cue and the target to be presented during search was manipulated.

> Material & Methods Participants 25 observers participated in the experiment. 17 participants were undergraduates (17 females; M = 25.5 years, SD = 5.99, 8 males; M = 27.8 years, SD = 6.08) from the University of Iceland who participated in this experiment for course credit and 8 staff members from the University of Iceland participated the experiment for gift card (3000 isk).

> All participants provided written informed consent and were tested for colorblindness with Ishihara's test for color deficiency (Ishihara, 2004) before the experiment.

> Participants were seated 57 cm away from a 24-inch monitor (ASUS, VX248h, resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels; refresh rate: 60 Hz).

> Participants were instructed to find the odd-colored target and report the location of the black dot (left or right) using the corresponding arrow keys (left/right arrow) on the keyboard.

> In the proceeding ensemble trial, participants were instructed to estimate the average orientation of the entire ensemble.

> Perceptual biases were found in the experiment showing that orientation judgements of the participants were biased towards the target color or away from the distractor color, in other words, the encoded attentional templates formed during the search task affected observers' ensemble estimates.

> In the Distractor Repeat and the Target Repeat condition both templates were active, but participants were only biased by the templates color which matched one of the subsets.

> However, in the Both Repeat condition participants were biased by both templates at the same time.

> On each block, participants completed an ensemble task which was preceded by 4-5 visual searches with identical target and distractor colors.

> Participants were asked to report the size of the target circle from the memorized array of colored circles.

> Importantly, their findings indicated that when participants were asked to report the size of an individual item rather than an ensemble average, task-relevant color grouping affected the representation of individual items.

> Our task required attentional selection guided by the color, and participants were expected to estimate average mean orientation of the lines.

Ethics approval statement:

> All experiments were done in agreement with the local ethics committee from the University of Iceland and the Declaration of Helsinki.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < 0.0125", "p > .05", "p < .01", 
"p < .02", "p < 0.05"), Text = c("However, a significant bias (after Bonferroni corrections, p < 0.0125) was found in Target Repeat when only the target color remained in the ensemble, t(24) = 3.40, p = .001, 95% CI [0.24, 0.99].", 
"Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction confirmed no significant differences between any of the conditions (all p > .05) (see Figure 3B).", 
"Finally, results revealed a significant orientation bias in the Both Repeat condition, t(29) = 6.16, p < .01, 95% CI [1.14, 2.27].", 
"Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons confirmed that all four conditions showed significantly lower variability at 500 ms compared to 150 ms (all p < .02).", 
"The results showed that there was a significant main effect of condition F(1, 29) = 11.32, p < 0.05, η²G = .067, indicating that the Both Repeat bias differed from the summed Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat bias across participants."
)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 96 columns across 2 data files.
#### Issues Identified
6 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("Study1_Exp1_AllRawData.csv", "Study1_Exp1_AllRawData.csv", "Study1_Exp1_AllRawData.csv", "Study1_Exp2_AllRawData.csv", "Study1_Exp2_AllRawData.csv", "Study1_Exp2_AllRawData.csv"), Column = c("V47", "gender", "meanBoth", "V48", "gender", "meanBoth"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 105600 values are missing", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: m/M", "👥 Colliding column names — Column name becomes \"meanBoth\" when special characters are replaced...", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 126720 values are missing", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: f/F", "👥 Colliding column names — Column name becomes \"meanBoth\" when special characters are replaced..." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: All experiments were done in agreement with the local ethics committee from the University of Iceland and the Declaration of Helsinki.
live_data_statements: Another study conducted by Alvarez and Oliva (2009) provided further evidence in favor of the attentionindependent nature of ensemble perception: While participants were attending and tracking a set of moving dots, they were still reliably able to detect orientation changes of an ensemble of Gabors in the unattended background.
They found that unattended ensembles affected performance only when their summary statistics matched the target category that the participants were searching for.
In Experiment 1, the participants were asked to look for the smallest or largest circle, thereby making size task relevant.
Before search, participants were given a visual cue that constituted the target template and the similarity between the cue and the target to be presented during search was manipulated.

Material & Methods Participants 25 observers participated in the experiment. 17 participants were undergraduates (17 females; M = 25.5 years, SD = 5.99, 8 males; M = 27.8 years, SD = 6.08) from the University of Iceland who participated in this experiment for course credit and 8 staff members from the University of Iceland participated the experiment for gift card (3000 isk).
All participants provided written informed consent and were tested for colorblindness with Ishihara's test for color deficiency (Ishihara, 2004) before the experiment.
Participants were seated 57 cm away from a 24-inch monitor (ASUS, VX248h, resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels; refresh rate: 60 Hz).
Participants were instructed to find the odd-colored target and report the location of the black dot (left or right) using the corresponding arrow keys (left/right arrow) on the keyboard.
In the proceeding ensemble trial, participants were instructed to estimate the average orientation of the entire ensemble.

Perceptual biases were found in the experiment showing that orientation judgements of the participants were biased towards the target color or away from the distractor color, in other words, the encoded attentional templates formed during the search task affected observers' ensemble estimates.
In the Distractor Repeat and the Target Repeat condition both templates were active, but participants were only biased by the templates color which matched one of the subsets.
However, in the Both Repeat condition participants were biased by both templates at the same time.
On each block, participants completed an ensemble task which was preceded by 4-5 visual searches with identical target and distractor colors.
Participants were asked to report the size of the target circle from the memorized array of colored circles.

Importantly, their findings indicated that when participants were asked to report the size of an individual item rather than an ensemble average, task-relevant color grouping affected the representation of individual items.
Our task required attentional selection guided by the color, and participants were expected to estimate average mean orientation of the lines.

text.text: Ensemble perception is a fundamental mechanism enabling the visual system to rapidly extract summary statistical properties (e.g., mean orientation) from a large number of objects.
This study investigated the influence of attentional templates for targets and distractors which are formed during visual search, on subsequent ensemble perception.
Participants first completed a visual search task involving target and distractor colors, followed by an ensemble orientation estimation task in which these colors recurred in various combinations.
The first experiment revealed that target template systematically biased ensemble estimates, with the strongest effect occurring when both template colors recurred together.

Furthermore, on these trials the bias exceeded the sum of the individual effects of target and distractor conditions, which demonstrates that combined effect of target enhancement and distractor suppression may be greater than predicted by their individual effects.
In the second experiment, presentation duration (150 ms vs. 500 ms) was manipulated.
While our results showed that duration did not alter the magnitude of the biases, a longer presentation time improved response precision.
These findings suggest that ensemble perception, can be modulated by recently formed attentional templates and systematically shape the formation of summary statistical representations.
In any natural scene, observers are constantly faced with a vast number of stimuli.
However, working memory capacity and attentional resources are limited which prevents the simultaneous or parallel processing of visual input.
When we look at a tree, we effortlessly perceive the leaves as uniformly "green" (Ahissar & Hochstein, 2004; Chong & Treisman, 2005).
text.formatted: When we look at a tree, we effortlessly perceive the leaves as uniformly "green" <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahissar & Hochstein, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chong & Treisman, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: This impression arises even though we cannot simultaneously encode the properties of every individual leaf.
Selectively processing or attending to the specific properties of each leaf is computationally demanding and severely capacity-limited (Tsotsos, 1988; Cowan, 2001).
text.formatted: Selectively processing or attending to the specific properties of each leaf is computationally demanding and severely capacity-limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Tsotsos, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Cowan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: To overcome these capacity limitations the visual system rapidly extracts statistical summaries, such as mean or variance, of a group of similar items to circumvent these limitations, a phenomenon known as ensemble perception (Ariely, 2001; Alvarez & Oliva, 2008; Alvarez, 2011; Whitney & Yamanashi Leib, 2018; Corbett et al., 2023).
text.formatted: To overcome these capacity limitations the visual system rapidly extracts statistical summaries, such as mean or variance, of a group of similar items to circumvent these limitations, a phenomenon known as ensemble perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ariely, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Alvarez & Oliva, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Alvarez, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Whitney & Yamanashi Leib, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Corbett et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Ensemble perception spans across feature levels: from low-level stimuli such as orientation (Dakin & Watt, 1997; Alvarez & Oliva, 2009), color (Maule et al., 2014; Bronfman, Brezis, Jacobson, & Usher, 2014), to mid-level stimuli such as size (Ariely, 2001), position (Morgan & Glennerster, 1991), but also to high-level stimuli such as emotional expressions (Haberman & Whitney, 2007; Haberman, Lee, & Whitney, 2015; Fischer & Whitney, 2011) and identity (de Fockert & Wolfenstein, 2009).
text.formatted: Ensemble perception spans across feature levels: from low-level stimuli such as orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dakin & Watt, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Alvarez & Oliva, 2009)</ref>, color <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Maule et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bronfman, Brezis, Jacobson, & Usher, 2014)</ref>, to mid-level stimuli such as size <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ariely, 2001)</ref>, position <ref type="bibr">(Morgan & Glennerster, 1991)</ref>, but also to high-level stimuli such as emotional expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Haberman & Whitney, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Haberman, Lee, & Whitney, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Fischer & Whitney, 2011)</ref> and identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(de Fockert & Wolfenstein, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Besides the mean of different features, second-order statistics such as variability (variance) or the range can also be extracted (Alvarez, 2011; Haberman et al., 2015; Khvostov & Utochkin, 2019) as well as more complex properties, such as the shapes of feature distributions (e.g., Chetverikov et al. 2016; Hansmann-Roth et al., 2021; see Chetverikov et al. 2019 for an overview).
text.formatted: Besides the mean of different features, second-order statistics such as variability (variance) or the range can also be extracted <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alvarez, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Haberman et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Khvostov & Utochkin, 2019)</ref> as well as more complex properties, such as the shapes of feature distributions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chetverikov et al. 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hansmann-Roth et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Chetverikov et al. 2019</ref> for an overview).

text.text: Ensemble perception was initially thought to be an automatic process that operates in parallel across the visual field without requiring selective attention or detailed encoding of each stimulus feature (Chong & Treisman 2005; Alvarez & Oliva, 2008; Alvarez & Oliva, 2009; Bronfman et al., 2014; Huang, 2015; Jackson-Nielsen et al., 2017; Khayat & Hochstein, 2018; Talipsky et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Ensemble perception was initially thought to be an automatic process that operates in parallel across the visual field without requiring selective attention or detailed encoding of each stimulus feature <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Chong & Treisman 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Alvarez & Oliva, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Alvarez & Oliva, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bronfman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Huang, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Jackson-Nielsen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Khayat & Hochstein, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Talipsky et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In their seminal paper, Ariely (2001) compared performance in two tasks: a member-identification and a mean-discrimination task, to understand how participants perceive individual circles or the mean size of the entire set.
text.formatted: In their seminal paper, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Ariely (2001)</ref> compared performance in two tasks: a member-identification and a mean-discrimination task, to understand how participants perceive individual circles or the mean size of the entire set.

text.text: Results showed that participants performed well on the mean-identification task, but their performance was near chance-level for the memberidentification task.
These results indicate that observers can extract summary statistics of a set without needing to remember all the details of the individual objects included in the set.
Therefore, ensemble representations are primarily based on summary statistics rather than on explicit representations of individual items.

In a follow-up study, Chong and Treisman (2005b) showed that averaging computations can occur automatically across perceptual groups, supporting parallel summary-statistic extraction rather than serial processing of individual items.
text.formatted: In a follow-up study, <ref type="bibr">Chong and Treisman (2005b)</ref> showed that averaging computations can occur automatically across perceptual groups, supporting parallel summary-statistic extraction rather than serial processing of individual items.

text.text: Another study conducted by Alvarez and Oliva (2009) provided further evidence in favor of the attentionindependent nature of ensemble perception: While participants were attending and tracking a set of moving dots, they were still reliably able to detect orientation changes of an ensemble of Gabors in the unattended background.
text.formatted: Another study conducted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Alvarez and Oliva (2009)</ref> provided further evidence in favor of the attentionindependent nature of ensemble perception: While participants were attending and tracking a set of moving dots, they were still reliably able to detect orientation changes of an ensemble of Gabors in the unattended background.

text.text: This indicates that spatial ensemble statistics can be extracted outside the focus of attention.
Moreover, findings from Posner cueing showed that judgement of the average speed of moving dots is persistent even when spatial attention is directed away from the ensemble (Talipsky et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Moreover, findings from Posner cueing showed that judgement of the average speed of moving dots is persistent even when spatial attention is directed away from the ensemble <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Talipsky et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, a set of other studies showed that ensemble perception does sometimes require attention. Jackson-Nielsen et al. (2017) implemented inattentional blindness paradigm and found that attention is necessary for ensemble perception.
text.formatted: Conversely, a set of other studies showed that ensemble perception does sometimes require attention. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Jackson-Nielsen et al. (2017)</ref> implemented inattentional blindness paradigm and found that attention is necessary for ensemble perception.

text.text: In a separate study, Dakin et al. (2009) showed that performance in judging the mean orientation of Gabor patches was significantly impaired when observers performed a concurrent attention-demanding task.
text.formatted: In a separate study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Dakin et al. (2009)</ref> showed that performance in judging the mean orientation of Gabor patches was significantly impaired when observers performed a concurrent attention-demanding task.

text.text: Similar findings were reported by Lukashevich et al. (2025), who examined whether ensemble perception requires attention.
text.formatted: Similar findings were reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Lukashevich et al. (2025)</ref>, who examined whether ensemble perception requires attention.

text.text: Participants either attended to changes in the mean orientation of ensembles or focused on a demanding central task while ignoring background ensembles that occasionally changed orientation.
Neural responses indicating change detection were only observed when participants attended to the ensembles.

The mean orientation of unattended ensemble was not automatically detected when attention was diverted from the central task, indicating that attention might be a key factor in the process of ensemble discrimination.

Another recent study by Kimchi and Sabary (2025) examined whether ensemble properties, such as the average size or average orientation, can be extracted from unattended stimuli using an inattention paradigm.
text.formatted: Another recent study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Kimchi and Sabary (2025)</ref> examined whether ensemble properties, such as the average size or average orientation, can be extracted from unattended stimuli using an inattention paradigm.

text.text: Participants performed a central change-detection task while a task-irrelevant background ensemble of circles or lines was presented simultaneously.
Across trials, average size or orientation changed independently, while individual elements continuously varied to prevent reliance on local cues.
Their results showed that changes in the ensemble mean were not detected when the stimuli were unattended.

Regardless of whether attention is required for ensemble perception, attentional allocation appears to influence the precision of ensemble processing and induces potential biases. Chong and Treisman (2005a) showed that the ensemble average is extracted more efficiently when attention is spread across the entire set while locally attending to individual items lead to impaired performance. Chen et al. (2021) investigated whether ensemble perception can occur outside of focal attention by examining the influence of a to-be-ignored ensemble on judgments of an attended ensemble.
text.formatted: Regardless of whether attention is required for ensemble perception, attentional allocation appears to influence the precision of ensemble processing and induces potential biases. <ref type="bibr">Chong and Treisman (2005a)</ref> showed that the ensemble average is extracted more efficiently when attention is spread across the entire set while locally attending to individual items lead to impaired performance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chen et al. (2021)</ref> investigated whether ensemble perception can occur outside of focal attention by examining the influence of a to-be-ignored ensemble on judgments of an attended ensemble.

text.text: They found that unattended ensembles affected performance only when their summary statistics matched the target category that the participants were searching for.
The authors concluded that ensemble processing outside the focus of attention depends on the observer's attentional control settings.

In a further exploration of the role of attention in ensemble perception, Baek and Chong (2020) proposed two attentional modes: distributed attention, which controls how we summarize statistically redundant information, and focused attention, which facilitates detailed object recognition and filters irrelevant input.
text.formatted: In a further exploration of the role of attention in ensemble perception, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Baek and Chong (2020)</ref> proposed two attentional modes: distributed attention, which controls how we summarize statistically redundant information, and focused attention, which facilitates detailed object recognition and filters irrelevant input.

text.text: Taken together, there is no solid consensus on the role of attention in ensemble perception, with evidence supporting both its dependent and automatic nature.
Attention may also influence ensemble perception by altering how strongly individual items contribute to the final summary representation.
Rather than weighting all items equally, certain stimuli appear to cause a disproportionate influence on ensemble estimates.
De Fockert and Marchant (2008) used an extra localization task to direct attention to a single item within a set of differently sized circles.
text.formatted: De <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Fockert and Marchant (2008)</ref> used an extra localization task to direct attention to a single item within a set of differently sized circles.

text.text: In Experiment 1, the participants were asked to look for the smallest or largest circle, thereby making size task relevant.
In Experiment 2, they instead looked for a circle defined by its brightness, which was either the smallest or the largest item in the group.
In both experiments, participants' average size estimates were systematically biased toward the size of the attended circle when attention was directed to the smallest or largest circle.

To directly examine whether salient items contribute disproportionately to ensemble representations, Kanaya et al. (2018) studied ensemble perception in both spatial and temporal ensembles to directly examine the role of saliency.
text.formatted: To directly examine whether salient items contribute disproportionately to ensemble representations, <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Kanaya et al. (2018)</ref> studied ensemble perception in both spatial and temporal ensembles to directly examine the role of saliency.

text.text: They investigated how observers perceive the mean size and temporal frequency of a set of discs.
Their findings indicated that objects which are highly salient are weighted more heavily (are amplified) within summary statistical representations and subsequently bias observers' estimates.

These findings suggest that ensemble perception is not a process of equal weighting across all items but instead, items that capture attention through their saliency contribute disproportionately to the ensemble representation.

Moreover, attentional biases can also arise from selection history (Theeuwes, 2018 (Theeuwes, , 2019)), whereby previous history of attentional selection influence subsequent attentional allocation independent of current goals or physical salience (Kristjánsson & Ásgeirsson, 2019; Maljkovic & Nakayama, 1994).
text.formatted: Moreover, attentional biases can also arise from selection history <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Theeuwes, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Theeuwes, , 2019))</ref>, whereby previous history of attentional selection influence subsequent attentional allocation independent of current goals or physical salience <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Kristjánsson & Ásgeirsson, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Maljkovic & Nakayama, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Selection history encompasses several experience-based influences on attention, including intertrial priming and reward learning (Theeuwes, 2018).
text.formatted: Selection history encompasses several experience-based influences on attention, including intertrial priming and reward learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Theeuwes, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: One example of selection history on ensemble processing was studied by Munneke et al. (2022).
text.formatted: One example of selection history on ensemble processing was studied by <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Munneke et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Their study focused on value-driven attentional capture through which previously rewarded stimuli can continue to attract attention even when they are irrelevant to the current task.

Participants estimated the average size of a group of circles, while one circle (either the smallest or largest) was presented in a color that had previously been associated with high, low or no reward.

The largest biases in perceived average size occurred when the largest circle had the highest reward value, with the amount of bias increasing linearly as reward magnitude increased even when dual-task conditions prevented the observer from fixating on the rewarded circle.
This research demonstrates that selection history can influence ensemble representations, with previously rewarded items contributing disproportionately to perceived ensemble averages.
Beyond attentional biases arising from selection history or visual salience, ensemble perception may also be shaped by representations actively maintained in visual working memory (VWM).
While selection history is the result of the influence of former experiences, representations in VWM can influence the processing of currently encountered information.

Selective attention relies on feature representations actively held in working memory to guide goaldirected behavior. Williams et al. (2021) examined whether VWM influences perceptual averaging when a subset of items matched a feature held in memory.
text.formatted: Selective attention relies on feature representations actively held in working memory to guide goaldirected behavior. <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Williams et al. (2021)</ref> examined whether VWM influences perceptual averaging when a subset of items matched a feature held in memory.

text.text: Participants performed a mean orientation task while concurrently maintaining a colored shape in VWM, which could match the color of a subset of items in the orientation ensemble display.
Specifically, they found that the perceived mean orientation was biased toward the average of the memory-matching colored subset of lines rather than the true mean of all items.
The information about memory-matching elements was more heavily weighed into the ensemble processing.
Therefore, the ensembles' contributions of individual items can be influenced by representations maintained for a concurrent VWM task.
Importantly, however, memory-matching representations constitute only one source of top-down attentional guidance.
Another fundamental mechanism is the use of attentional templates that guide visual search toward behaviorally relevant information.

Attentional templates, unlike the one maintained for the concurrent memory task in the paper by Williams et al. (2021), are representations of features used to select relevant information for visual search.
text.formatted: Attentional templates, unlike the one maintained for the concurrent memory task in the paper by <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Williams et al. (2021)</ref>, are representations of features used to select relevant information for visual search.

text.text: However, far less is known about the influence of these attentional templates on ensemble perception.
Attentional templates are defined as mental representations of target-defining features, which are used to guide attention and determine whether any given stimulus in the scene qualifies as a target.
Attentional templates can be inferred and modified over time with a search task and indicate features that differentiate targets from distractors.
This idea originates from early theories of visual search, which proposed that attention is guided by an internal description of target-defining features.

According to Duncan and Humphreys (1989), visual inputs receive greater attentional weight to the extent that they match this internal representation, thereby facilitating the selection of behaviorally relevant information during visual search.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Duncan and Humphreys (1989)</ref>, visual inputs receive greater attentional weight to the extent that they match this internal representation, thereby facilitating the selection of behaviorally relevant information during visual search.

text.text: Attentional control may be mediated by positive templates that increase target-matching information and by negative templates (or templates for rejection) that facilitate the exclusion of information about known distractors (Arita et al., 2012; Carlisle, 2023).
text.formatted: Attentional control may be mediated by positive templates that increase target-matching information and by negative templates (or templates for rejection) that facilitate the exclusion of information about known distractors <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Carlisle, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Imagine you have lost and are searching for your cat (target template) amongst other cats (distractor templates) on the street.
To do so, you need to rely on your templates about your own cat like the color of its collar, the specific feature of its fur, etc.
Top-down knowledge about the target guides visual search by biasing attention toward stimuli that match target-defining features (Vickery et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Top-down knowledge about the target guides visual search by biasing attention toward stimuli that match target-defining features <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Vickery et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Hout and Goldinger (2015) demonstrated that the precision and sharpness of target templates directly influence visual search performance.
Before search, participants were given a visual cue that constituted the target template and the similarity between the cue and the target to be presented during search was manipulated.
More precise and distinct target representations optimize attentional guidance and accelerate decision-making processes.
When template precision decreased, participants' performance decreased systematically, and this cost was proportional to the dissimilarity between the target cue and the actual target.

Using eye tracking, the authors further showed that degraded templates increased the number of locations observers fixated before finding the target and reduced the efficiency of target verification after fixation.
Similarly, Lau et al. (2021) showed that target-distractor discriminability shapes template formation, with lower discriminability leading observers to develop higher-resolution target templates.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Lau et al. (2021)</ref> showed that target-distractor discriminability shapes template formation, with lower discriminability leading observers to develop higher-resolution target templates.

text.text: The targets were repeatedly searched against distractors that varied in their visual similarity to the targets.

Search among easily discriminable targets and distractors led to relatively coarse templates of the targets, while difficult search (which required target-similar distractors) led to the formation of higherresolution target templates.

This is also consistent with the findings of Geng et al., (2017), and Yu and Geng (2019) that the target template can also be systematically shifted by distractor context. Geng et al. (2017) found that frequent exposure to highly target similar distractors can produced a narrower target representation.
text.formatted: This is also consistent with the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Geng et al., (2017)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Yu and Geng (2019)</ref> that the target template can also be systematically shifted by distractor context. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Geng et al. (2017)</ref> found that frequent exposure to highly target similar distractors can produced a narrower target representation.

text.text: Building on these findings, Yu and Geng (2019) demonstrated that predictable distractor context caused a shift in the representation of the target away from the distractor features, whereas highly similar distractors also produce asymmetric sharpening of the target template.
text.formatted: Building on these findings, <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Yu and Geng (2019)</ref> demonstrated that predictable distractor context caused a shift in the representation of the target away from the distractor features, whereas highly similar distractors also produce asymmetric sharpening of the target template.

text.text: These changes made the targets stand out more from the distractors and enhanced the visual search.

Besides target templates, there are also negative or rejection templates that can be used to help reject distractors by providing information about irrelevant features, as previously discussed. Arita et al. (2012) proposed that attention can be actively directed away from irrelevant items, providing one of the first demonstrations that observers can use distractor information to guide selection.
text.formatted: Besides target templates, there are also negative or rejection templates that can be used to help reject distractors by providing information about irrelevant features, as previously discussed. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Arita et al. (2012)</ref> proposed that attention can be actively directed away from irrelevant items, providing one of the first demonstrations that observers can use distractor information to guide selection.

text.text: Evidence from Carlisle and Nitka (2019) further suggests that both positive and negative templates can guide attention, however, there are mechanisms that may be different with negative templates than with the positive templates. (Carlisle, 2023).
text.formatted: Evidence from <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Carlisle and Nitka (2019)</ref> further suggests that both positive and negative templates can guide attention, however, there are mechanisms that may be different with negative templates than with the positive templates. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carlisle, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies demonstrate that attentional guidance can use the information from both targets and distractors during visual search.
However, it remains unknown whether such template-based biases in attentional selection also apply to the integration of multiple objects such as when ensemble representations are formed.

Attentional templates could influence the processing of individual ensemble items, and items that match the target and distractor features could contribute differently to the computation of the perceived average, leading to systematic biases in ensemble estimates.
Some previous work showed that attentional selection continues to influence perception following visual search trials (Rafiei et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Some previous work showed that attentional selection continues to influence perception following visual search trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Rafiei et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The study showed that information selected and rejected during visual search biased subsequent perceptual judgments.
This suggests that attentional selection leaves persistent traces in perception.
It remains unclear, however, whether these opposing effect of target selection and distractor rejection extend to carry over to judgements of the statistical summaries of ensembles.
Building on this question, our study investigates whether attentional templates, both templates for distractors and targets, jointly influence ensemble processing.

To explore this, the two subsets of oriented lines within each ensemble display were oriented in different directions, one 15° clockwise, and the other 15° counterclockwise, from the global ensemble mean.

Each ensemble judgment was preceded by 4 to 5 visual search trials where both the target and distractor colors were fixed so that representations of the same colors, allowing target-and distractor-related representations to develop across successive searches.
We predicted that attentional templates formed during searches would bias subsequent ensemble processing.

Specifically, if target and distractor representations differentially influence the weighting of ensemble items, perceived mean orientation should be systematically shifted depending on whether the target color, distractor color, or both reappeared in the subsequent ensemble display.

The experiment was carried out using Psychopy 2021.1.4 (Peirce et al., 2019) and stimuli were presented on a dark gray background (luminance = 20 cd/m²).

Each block consisted of 4-5 search trials and a single ensemble task where observers were asked to report the average orientation of the ensembles (See Figure 1).

text.text: Participants were instructed to find the odd-colored target and report the location of the black dot (left or right) using the corresponding arrow keys (left/right arrow) on the keyboard.
In the proceeding ensemble trial, participants were instructed to estimate the average orientation of the entire ensemble.
Immediately after the ensemble display disappeared, a white adjustment line (line length: 2.5°; line width = 3 pixels) appeared at the center of the screen.
This line served as a response tool and remained visible until the participant confirmed their adjustment by pressing the space bar.
The initial orientation of the adjustment line was randomly selected on each trial from a uniform distribution between 0° and 179°.
The entire experiment lasted around 80 minutes.
The experiment was preceded by an initial training consisting of 10 blocks, but the data was not analyzed from this training.
Participants could take breaks every 10 to 12 minutes.
Each trial started with a 500 ms fixation cross followed by 4-5 search displays.

Afterwards, the ensemble display appeared for 200 ms followed by an adjustment task which participants required to adjust the white line in the center of the display to match the average orientation of the entire ensemble from the previous display.
Each block began with a fixation on a white thin central cross (0.5° × 0.5°) for 500 ms, followed by four to five visual search trials and a single orientation ensemble display.
In each visual search trial, nine diamond-shaped stimuli (1.5° × 1.5°) appeared on the screen: one target and eight distractors.
Each diamond had a small black dot (0.1° × 0.1°) located either on its left or right corner.
The target was defined by its color, which differed from that of the distractors.

Four colors were selected to serve as potential target and distractor colors, corresponding to four positions on a 48 isoluminant (Witzel & Gegenfurtner, 2013 , 2015) DKL color wheel: 0, 12, 24, and 36 JNDs (red, green, yellow and purple).
text.formatted: Four colors were selected to serve as potential target and distractor colors, corresponding to four positions on a 48 isoluminant <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Witzel & Gegenfurtner, 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2015)</ref> DKL color wheel: 0, 12, 24, and 36 JNDs (red, green, yellow and purple).

text.text: Distractor colors were always 12 JND away from the target color.

Therefore, the experiment included eight color combinations (Target-Distractor) from the color wheel: 0-12, 12-24, 24-36, 36-48, 12-0, 24-12, 36-24, 48-36. All diamonds were presented at random locations within an invisible square on the screen.
text.formatted: Therefore, the experiment included eight color combinations (Target-Distractor) from the color wheel: 0-12, <ref type="bibr">12-24, 24-36, 36-48, 12-0, 24-12, 36-24, 48-36.</ref> All diamonds were presented at random locations within an invisible square on the screen.

text.text: Stimulus positions were generated from two coordinate sets, each spanning -12° to +12° of visual angle in 2° increments.
The x-and y-coordinate sets were independently shuffled on each trial.
This ensured random but non-overlapping positions, while keeping all stimuli within a fixed display area.
Following the search trials, an ensemble display consisting of twelve colored lines (2° × 0.3°) was presented for 200 ms.
The spatial arrangement of the lines was determined using the same possible combinations as for the diamonds on the search trials.
Two equally numbered subsets of lines made up this display (six lines per subset); the colors were determined by pairings of different colors.

These colors were selected to create four different conditions: 1) the Both Repeat condition: the two subsets of lines contained the same colors as the targets and distractors from the preceding search tasks, 2) the Distractor Repeat condition: one of the two subsets contained the distractor color from the preceding search block and the second subset color was a new color, 3) the Target Repeat condition: one of the two subsets of lines had the target color from the preceding search block and the second subset color was a new color and 4) Control condition: both colors of the subset were new colors that were not presented on the preceding search task.

For example, if the target color was purple and distractors were green, Target Repeat condition had purple and red, Distractor Repeat condition had green and yellow, Both Repeat condition had purple and green and lastly control condition red and yellow.

Besides differing in color, the two subsets also had distinct average orientations following the design by Williams et al. (2021): One subset was oriented 15° clockwise (CW) from the global mean of the entire set, while the other subset was oriented 15° counterclockwise (CCW) from the global mean (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: Besides differing in color, the two subsets also had distinct average orientations following the design by <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Williams et al. (2021)</ref>: One subset was oriented 15° clockwise (CW) from the global mean of the entire set, while the other subset was oriented 15° counterclockwise (CCW) from the global mean (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Within a subset, the orientation range spanned 30 degrees.
The mean orientation of the overall set was selected from six predefined means: 15°, 45°, 75°, 105°, 135°, and 165° to ensure that the same global means were presented across all four conditions.
We examined response errors by calculating the differences between observers estimated global mean and the actual global mean orientation of the 12 presented lines bounded to +/-90°.
Trials were excluded if observers' adjustment errors were larger than 3 standard deviations from their average adjustment error.

The average response errors and the variability of the response errors were first calculated using circular statistics with the circular package in R. These values were calculated for each of the four conditions and separately for the CCW and CW condition.
A bias towards the counterclockwise subset or a bias towards the clockwise subset have opposite signs; however, their meaning is identical.
So, we flipped the sign of the CCW condition to match the CW condition and to extract a single bias value towards or away from any of the ensemble subsets.

text.text: To examine whether attentional priming or color changes influenced the variability of orientation judgments, a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted to compare the response variability (circular standard deviation (CSD)) across conditions.

The analysis revealed no significant main effect of condition on variability, F(3, 72) = 0.688, p = .561, η²G = 0.0005, indicating that variability in orientation judgments did not significantly differ across the four conditions.
Descriptive statistics showed that mean variability values were highly similar across all conditions, all range in between 12.15° and 12.30°.
Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction confirmed no significant differences between any of the conditions (all p > .05) (see Figure 3B).

text.text: In the Both Repeat condition, both the target and distractor colors remained in the ensemble, whereas only one of these colors remained in the Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat conditions.

If the effects of target enhancement and distractor suppression in the ensemble task are additive, the bias observed in the Both Repeat condition should equal the sum of the biases observed in the Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat conditions.

To test this prediction, we computed the summed bias (Target Repeat + Distractor Repeat) for each participant and compared it with the observed bias in the Both Repeat condition using a paired-samples t-test.

The results indicated that the bias observed in the Both Repeat condition was significantly larger than the additive prediction obtained by summing the biases, t(24) = 2.94, p = .007, 95% CI [0.29, 1.65], Hedges's g = 1.85 (large).

This difference was supported by the Bayes Factor as well (BF₁₀ > 6.34), indicating moderate evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis that the bias in the Both Repeat condition differed from the summed bias predicted by the Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat conditions.

text.text: Experiment 1 investigated how target and distractor templates formed during a visual search task affect the extraction of summary statistics.

To analyze the effect of the templates simultaneously, observers completed search tasks which included 9 diamonds (one target and eight distractors) and 12 lines were shown in the ensemble display for 200 ms, right before the adjustment task.

Perceptual biases were found in the experiment showing that orientation judgements of the participants were biased towards the target color or away from the distractor color, in other words, the encoded attentional templates formed during the search task affected observers' ensemble estimates.

This indicates that the attentional templates formed during visual search remained even after the search task had ended and continued to shape how information was combined while performing ensemble perception tasks.
Our results showed that the perceptual bias was strongest in the Both Repeat (the target and distractor colors remain unchanged) condition, as indicated by the largest bias.
In the Distractor Repeat and the Target Repeat condition both templates were active, but participants were only biased by the templates color which matched one of the subsets.
However, in the Both Repeat condition participants were biased by both templates at the same time.
The effect of using both templates simultaneously may lead to a larger bias in observers' averaging judgements.
One possible explanation is that target enhancement and distractor suppression work simultaneously, each further enhancing the weighting of template-matching information in ensemble computations.
Rather than working independently, the target enhancement and the distractor suppression appear to reinforce one another, resulting in a stronger bias when both templates are active together.
In contrast, when neither color was previously seen (Control condition) no bias was observed.
The conditions in which only one of the colors remained produced intermediate levels of bias.

Notably, the Target Repeat condition yielded a stronger and statistically significant bias compared to the Distractor Repeat condition, which showed a smaller effect that did not survive Bonferroni correction.

This finding may be attributed to the higher priority given to target information during visual search, and to the fact that target templates typically enhance attentional processing, whereas distractor templates can be used to guide attention away from irrelevant information.
Importantly, previous studies have shown that the effects of negative-templates tend to be weaker than the effects of positive-templates (Arita et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Importantly, previous studies have shown that the effects of negative-templates tend to be weaker than the effects of positive-templates <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Zhang et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This imbalance in attentional guidance may therefore have transferred to the next ensemble task, leading to a stronger target-related than distractor-related bias.

Overall, it can be concluded that previously formed attentional templates affected the subsequent ensemble estimation, the greatest bias being found when both the target-matching information and the distractor-matching information were present.
Additionally, no differences in the variability of ensemble orientation judgements were observed across conditions.
The result showed that the effect of condition on CSD was not significant as reported.

If observers were paying attention to a single color subset, the range of the orientations contributing to their estimate would have been smaller than if they were paying attention to orientations from both subsets.

This is likely to result in less response variability in one-subset-based estimates than in estimates relying on the integration of information from both subsets (Khvostov and Utochkin, 2019; Khvostov et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is likely to result in less response variability in one-subset-based estimates than in estimates relying on the integration of information from both subsets <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Khvostov and Utochkin, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Khvostov et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, no differences in response variability across conditions suggests that response variability was similar even though there was a template related bias in the perceived average orientation.
Target and distractor templates from a search task can bias subsequent ensemble estimates.
Our results from Experiment 1 suggest that observers' orientation averages were biased towards the target color and to a much weaker extent away from the distractor color.
As a result, the estimated orientation averages were biased towards the average of the subset that contained the target color and away from the subset that contained the distractor color.
Experiment 2 was thus designed to determine if these template-induced biases varied with the duration of the ensemble presentation.
In Experiment 1, the ensemble display was presented for 200 ms.

It has been shown that summary statistics can be extracted from briefly presented displays (Li et al., 2016), while the influence of items on ensemble judgments may encode differently across presentation times.
text.formatted: It has been shown that summary statistics can be extracted from briefly presented displays <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Li et al., 2016)</ref>, while the influence of items on ensemble judgments may encode differently across presentation times.

text.text: With shorter presentation times, observers might not have enough time to distribute attention over the ensemble, and items in the template matching category might be given more attention.
The longer the presentation time is, the more time the observers could process the rest of the items, which may minimize the template-matching subset bias.
Or perhaps, if given more time to observe, the observers could continue to be biased toward template-matching items, leading to a stronger bias.
Previous studies have examined how presentation duration affects biases in ensemble judgments, with mixed results.
For example, Goldenberg et al. (2021) found that both positive and negative facial expressions were amplified in judgments of mean emotion.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Goldenberg et al. (2021)</ref> found that both positive and negative facial expressions were amplified in judgments of mean emotion.

text.text: However, the amplification of positive expressions developed more slowly, requiring longer presentation times to reach a magnitude comparable to that observed for negative expressions.
In contrast, Williams et al. (2021) compared ensemble presentation durations of 150 ms and 500 ms but did not find any differences in the magnitude of the VWM-related bias.
text.formatted: In contrast, <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Williams et al. (2021)</ref> compared ensemble presentation durations of 150 ms and 500 ms but did not find any differences in the magnitude of the VWM-related bias.

text.text: These findings suggest that the influence of presentation duration on ensemble judgments may depend on the source of the bias.
However, neither study directly addressed whether additional processing time strengthens biases arising from attentional templates established during visual search.

We thus investigated whether attentional templates created during the visual search task affected subsequent ensemble estimation differently at a short (150 ms) and a longer (500 ms) presentation time in Experiment 2.

text.text: All experiments were done in agreement with the local ethics committee from the University of Iceland and the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants were seated 57 cm away from a 24-inch monitor (ASUS, VX248h, resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels; refresh rate: 60 Hz).
The experiment was carried out using Psychopy 2021.1.4 (Peirce et al., 2019) and stimuli were presented on a dark gray background (luminance = 20 cd/m²).
text.formatted: The experiment was carried out using Psychopy 2021.1.4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Peirce et al., 2019)</ref> and stimuli were presented on a dark gray background (luminance = 20 cd/m²).

text.text: The display was color-calibrated using a Cambridge Research Systems ColorCal MKII photometer.
The procedure and the design of Experiment 2 was identical to Experiment 1.
In Experiment 2, we manipulated the presentation time of the lines (150 ms vs 500 ms).

To be able to equalize the number of trials (and keep the experiment length within a reasonable amount of time) in each condition we reduced the number of color combinations in Experiment 2 but the total number of blocks remained identical.
Color combinations for targets and distractors that were used in Experiment 2 are: 0 -12, 36-24, 12-0, 24-36).
text.formatted: Color combinations for targets and distractors that were used in Experiment 2 are: 0 <ref type="bibr">-12, 36-24, 12-0, 24-36)</ref>.

text.text: The entire experiment lasted around 80 minutes.
The experiment was preceded by an initial training phase consisting of 10 blocks but the data was not collected from participants during this training.
Participants could take breaks every 10 to 12 minutes.
On each block, participants completed an ensemble task which was preceded by 4-5 visual searches with identical target and distractor colors.
As previously, this allowed us to test how prior attentional selection (target priming and distractor suppression) influenced perceived average orientation.

These orientation judgments were performed under a short (150 ms) and a long (500 ms) presentation time across the same four within-subject conditions as in Experiment 1: Control, Distractor Repeat, Target Repeat, and Both Repeat.

First, one-sample t-tests were conducted separately for each condition and collapsed across presentation times to determine if the biases toward or away from the subset were significantly different from zero.
Results showed that in the Control condition there was no evidence of a bias, t(29) = -0.17, p = .87, 95% CI [-0.37, 0.33].
Additionally, in the Target Repeat condition, the observed bias was modest but significant before correction, t(29) = 2.24, p = .03, 95% CI [0.04, 0.79].
The Distractor Repeat condition did show a visibly small but not significant bias, t(29) = 1.79, p = .08, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.62].
Finally, results revealed a significant orientation bias in the Both Repeat condition, t(29) = 6.16, p < .01, 95% CI [1.14, 2.27].
text.formatted: Finally, results revealed a significant orientation bias in the Both Repeat condition, t(29) = 6.16, p < .01, 95% CI [1.14, 2.27].

text.text: This effect remained significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, indicating a reliable orientation bias in this condition (see Figure 5A).
text.formatted: This effect remained significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, indicating a reliable orientation bias in this condition (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5A</ref>).

text.text: We next examined whether the magnitude of orientation bias differed across conditions and presentation times.
A 2 (presentation time) × 4 (conditions) repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted on the average orientation adjustment bias.

The analysis revealed a significant main effect of condition, F(3, 87) = 17.3, p < .001, η²G =.17, indicating that orientation bias differed across experimental conditions but there was no main effect of presentation time, F(1, 29) = 0.9, p = .34, η²G = .004, nor a significant interaction between condition and presentation time, F(3, 87) = 0.38, p = .76, η²G =.004.
text.formatted: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of condition, F(3, 87) = 17.3, p < .001, η²G =.17, indicating that orientation bias differed across experimental conditions but there was no main effect of presentation time, F(1, 29) = 0.9, p = .34, η²G = .004, nor a significant interaction between condition and presentation time, F(3, 87) = 0.38, p = .76, η²G =.004.

text.text: A Bayesian model comparison supported these results.
The model including Condition alone received the strongest support, whereas adding presentation time or the Condition × Presentation Time interaction did not provide a better fit to the data.
Thus, the Bayesian analysis provided further evidence that variation in orientation bias was primarily associated with condition rather than presentation time.
Together, these results indicate that observed orientation biases were influenced by the four different conditions, while presentation time had no impact on the bias magnitude (see Figure 5B).
text.formatted: Together, these results indicate that observed orientation biases were influenced by the four different conditions, while presentation time had no impact on the bias magnitude (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5B</ref>).

text.text: To examine how stimulus duration and attentional templates influence the precision of ensemble orientation estimates, we analyzed the variability in the adjustment responses using the circular standard deviation (CSD) across conditions and presentation times (e.g., whether repeating the target or distractor color affected the variability of participants' orientation responses).
A 2 (presentation time) × 4 (condition) repeated-measures ANOVA was conducted on the circular standard deviation of orientation responses.

The analysis revealed a significant main effect of presentation time, F(1, 29) = 19.22, p <.001, η²G=.13, with circular SD being consistently smaller at 500 ms than at 150 ms across conditions (see Figure 6).
text.formatted: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of presentation time, F(1, 29) = 19.22, p <.001, η²G=.13, with circular SD being consistently smaller at 500 ms than at 150 ms across conditions (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">6</ref>).

text.text: As shown in Figure 6, the striped bars in the Figure 6 (500 ms, M = 10.9°, SEM = 0.95) consistently fall below the corresponding solid bars (150 ms, M = 14.9°, SEM = 0.95) for each condition.

text.text: Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons confirmed that all four conditions showed significantly lower variability at 500 ms compared to 150 ms (all p < .02).
text.formatted: Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons confirmed that all four conditions showed significantly lower variability at 500 ms compared to 150 ms (all p < .02).

text.text: There was no significant effect of condition, F(1.76, 51.16) = 1.46, p = .241, η²G = .001 and the interaction between presentation time and condition also was not significant, F(2.17, 63.00) = 1.12, p = .336, η²G < .001, suggesting that the effect of duration on response variability did not differ across conditions.
