text.text: Descriptively, response variability was lower at 500 ms than at 150 ms when averaged across conditions (see Figure 6).
text.formatted: Descriptively, response variability was lower at 500 ms than at 150 ms when averaged across conditions (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">6</ref>).

text.text: In summary, longer presentation time substantially improved the precision of ensemble orientation estimates, whereas response variability did not differ significantly between the attentional-template conditions.

We compared the Both Repeat bias to the sum of the Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat biases for the two presentation times to determine whether the Both Repeat bias could be attributed to additive effects of the Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat biases.
First, a 2 (presentation time) × 2 (Both Repeat condition and Sum of Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat conditions) repeatedmeasures ANOVA was conducted.

The results showed that there was a significant main effect of condition F(1, 29) = 11.32, p < 0.05, η²G = .067, indicating that the Both Repeat bias differed from the summed Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat bias across participants.
text.formatted: The results showed that there was a significant main effect of condition F(1, 29) = 11.32, p < 0.05, η²G = .067, indicating that the Both Repeat bias differed from the summed Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat bias across participants.

text.text: There was no significant main effect of presentation time, F(1, 29) = 0.75, p = .394, η²G = .008, and no significant Presentation Time × Condition interaction, F(1, 29) = 0.29, p = .592, η²G = .001.

The nonsignificant interaction indicated that the difference between the Both Repeat bias and the summed Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat bias did not significantly vary across presentation times (see Figure 7).
text.formatted: The nonsignificant interaction indicated that the difference between the Both Repeat bias and the summed Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat bias did not significantly vary across presentation times (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">7</ref>).

text.text: To examine these comparisons separately at each presentation time, paired-samples t-tests were conducted.

For 150 ms, there was no significant difference between the Both Repeat condition and the sum of the Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat conditions, t(29) = 2.02, p = .052, 95% CI[-0.01, 1.73], Hedges's g = 0.41.
The Bayes factor (BF₁₀ = 1.15) indicated only weak evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
For 500 ms, the Both Repeat condition bias was significantly larger than the sum of the Distractor Repeat and Target Repeat conditions, t(29) = 3.12, p = .004, 95% CI[0.39, 1.90], Hedges's g = 0.64.
The Bayes Factor (BF₁₀ = 9.68) provided moderate to strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
Although the evidence for a super-additive bias was stronger at 500 ms, the Both Repeat bias was numerically larger than the sum of the individual biases at both presentation times (see Figure 7).
text.formatted: Although the evidence for a super-additive bias was stronger at 500 ms, the Both Repeat bias was numerically larger than the sum of the individual biases at both presentation times (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">7</ref>).

text.text: Moreover, the nonsignificant interaction indicated that there was no statistically reliable difference in the magnitude of the super-additive effect between presentation times.

The goal of Experiment 2 was to determine whether changes in the presentation time of the ensemble display modulate the bias exerted by the previously formed attentional templates from the search task, as observed in Experiment 1.
The primary finding was that presentation time did not significantly affect the magnitude of the observed orientation biases.
The orientation bias significantly differed between conditions as in Experiment 1.

Participants' orientation judgements were more biased in the Both Repeat condition than in the other conditions, which was also evident in Experiment 1. replicating the pattern observed in Experiment 1.

This suggests that the influence of attentional templates on ensemble judgements is relatively stable across the presentation durations tested, rather than becoming stronger with additional processing time.
As in Experiment 1, response variability did not differ significantly between conditions, although it was generally lower at 500 ms than at 150 ms.

Furthermore, although the super-additive effect reached significance only at 500 ms, there was no significant interaction with presentation time, suggesting that the magnitude of this effect did not reliably differ between presentation durations.
Across two experiments, we investigated whether judgments of mean orientation in ensembles of colored lines were biased by attentional templates formed during a preceding visual search task.

If attentional templates of distractors and targets are formed during the visual search task and are still active in the ensemble task, we expected orientation averages to be biased when subsets of the ensemble match the active template colors.

We implemented four conditions: 1) the Target Repeat condition where one of the two subsets of lines had the target color from the preceding search block and the second subset color was a new color, 2) the Distractor Repeat condition where one of the two subsets contained the distractor color from the preceding search block and the second subset color was a new color, 3) the Both Repeat condition where the two subsets of lines contained the same colors as the targets and distractors from the preceding search tasks, and 4) the Control condition where both colors of the subset were new colors that were not presented on the preceding search task.
In the Both Repeat condition there are two biases simultaneously working together: one repulsive bias away from the distractor color and the other one is attractive bias towards the target color.
Consequently, this condition exhibited the strongest bias in both experiments compared to the Target or Distractor Repeat conditions.
Repeating the target color alone (Target Repeat condition) resulted in a larger bias than the distractor color alone (Distractor Repeat condition).

However, only the Target Repeat bias remained significant when correcting for multiple comparisons, while the Distractor Repeat bias, although visible, was not significant when using Bonferroni correction.
We examined how well the Both Repeat condition could be predicted by the combined effect of the Distractor Repeat and the Target Repeat conditions.

The results showed that the bias was significantly larger when both colors remained identical than the additive prediction by summing the bias from the Target Repeat and the Distractor Repeat conditions in Experiment 1.
In Experiment 2, the Both Repeat bias was numerically larger than the sum of the individual biases at both presentation times, although the difference reached statistical significance only at 500 ms.
Furthermore, the different presentation times in the Experiment 2 showed no effect on the magnitude of the biases.
The results of our study are in line with Williams et al. (2021).
text.formatted: The results of our study are in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Williams et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: They showed that reports of mean orientation were biased toward the mean orientation of the same-color subset that participants needed to maintain in VWM.
Critically, however, the present experiments involved active attentional templates for color subsets that were formed during a preceding visual search task.

Accordingly, both of our experiments showed that when the target color reappeared in the ensemble display, reports of orientation averages were more biased toward the orientation of the target-color subset.
A related effect of task-relevant color information was demonstrated by Brady and Alvarez (2011).
text.formatted: A related effect of task-relevant color information was demonstrated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Brady and Alvarez (2011)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were asked to report the size of the target circle from the memorized array of colored circles.
It was found that responses were biased by the sizes of the circles that shared the color of the target.

Importantly, their findings indicated that when participants were asked to report the size of an individual item rather than an ensemble average, task-relevant color grouping affected the representation of individual items.
Here, we build on that relationship by examining how attentional priority to a task-relevant color can affect the subsequent ensemble estimate.
This template-driven weighting is in line with the evidence that ensemble perception is sensitive to the priority of items.
Iakovlev and Utochkin (2020) showed that more perceptually salient items demonstrate a stronger influence on mean estimates than less salient items.

Despite our focus on top-down attentional priority, and their focus on bottom-up perceptual salience, our results provide new evidence that unequal weighting can also occur when item priority is determined by top-down attentional goals.
Specifically, items that matched the target template had more weight in the ensemble estimate, while items that matched the distractor template seemed to have less weight in the ensemble estimate.
However, we cannot explain the strongest bias in the Both Repeat condition simply by unequal weighting.

The bias in the Both Repeat condition was larger than the sum of the biases in the two conditions (Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat), suggesting that the simultaneous presence of both the target and distractor colors may reflect an interaction between target enhancement and distractor suppression.
Our data suggests that target-related templates bias ensemble judgements to a greater degree than distractor-related templates.
This difference may be explained by how attentional templates work in visual search.
Target templates can direct attention to task-relevant information, while distractor-related information can be used to suppress or reject irrelevant information (Gaspelin & Luck, 2018).
text.formatted: Target templates can direct attention to task-relevant information, while distractor-related information can be used to suppress or reject irrelevant information <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gaspelin & Luck, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: While both target and distractor can be equally informative, positive templates could be more effective on attentional guidance, and negative templates have been found to be less effective and more task-dependent (Arita et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2020; Carlisle, 2023).
text.formatted: While both target and distractor can be equally informative, positive templates could be more effective on attentional guidance, and negative templates have been found to be less effective and more task-dependent <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Arita et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Zhang et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Carlisle, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The strong target-related bias found in the current study can be explained by this asymmetry between positive and negative templates, as the target template created in the visual search task might have had a greater carry-over effect for the subsequent ensemble judgement than the distractor template.

At the same time, orientation judgments were not fully determined by the repeated (template-matching) colors, as evidenced by the intermediate biases in the Target Repeat and Distractor Repeat conditions.
This is consistent with a weighted sampling mechanism.
Attentional templates modulate how strongly each subset contributes to the ensemble representation, without the influence of the remaining items being completely overridden.
In Experiment 2 we manipulated the presentation times of the ensembles.
In the present study, presentation time could affect template-based biases in two possible ways.
If the additional processing time allows participants to continue prioritizing the subset where the template-matching occurs, the bias may become even larger at 500 ms.
On the other hand, if the participants pay attention to the template-matching subset first, the extra time at 500 ms may redistribute attention across the entire ensemble, reducing the initial bias.
We found no difference in the strength of the bias between the short and long presentation times.
The template-based bias was already apparent at 150 ms and showed a little change at 500 ms, indicating that further processing time did not significantly alter the extent of the bias.

Thus neither of the two predicted effects was observed: longer presentation time neither reinforced the template-based bias nor weakened it through a redistribution of attention across the ensemble display.
On the other hand, Williams et al. (2021) investigated whether the memory-matching bias was due to the strategic allocation of attention using short and long ensemble presentation times.
text.formatted: On the other hand, <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Williams et al. (2021)</ref> investigated whether the memory-matching bias was due to the strategic allocation of attention using short and long ensemble presentation times.

text.text: They assumed that voluntary attentional allocation would be more difficult at shorter presentation times, and that a strategically driven bias should, accordingly, grow stronger with longer presentation times.
However, this strategic account was specific to their VWM task, in which participants could strategically attend to memorymatching items to improve their memory performance.

Previous studies, however, indicate that the effects of attention on ensemble perception may vary depending on the presentation time (Haberman & Whitney, 2010; Li et al., 2016; Goldenberg et al., 2021). Goldenberg et al. (2021) found that while positive and negative faces were amplified in mean emotion judgements, longer presentation times were needed for the bias towards positive faces to reach the level of the bias towards the negative faces.
text.formatted: Previous studies, however, indicate that the effects of attention on ensemble perception may vary depending on the presentation time <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Haberman & Whitney, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Li et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Goldenberg et al., 2021)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Goldenberg et al. (2021)</ref> found that while positive and negative faces were amplified in mean emotion judgements, longer presentation times were needed for the bias towards positive faces to reach the level of the bias towards the negative faces.

text.text: Our results, however, indicate that template-based biases formed from earlier visual search are relatively stable over the different presentation times used here.
The difference might be due to different types of attentional priority tested in the two studies or to the different presentation times employed.
Additionally, we tested whether the bias in the Both Repeat condition was merely an additive combination of the biases measured in the Target Repeat and the Distractor Repeat conditions.
In the Target Repeat condition, the target color from the previous search task was present in the ensemble while the distractor color was replaced by a new color.
In contrast, in the Distractor Repeat condition, the distractor color remained unchanged while the target color has changed.
In the Both Repeat condition, both the target and distractor colors from the preceding search task were used to create the two subsets in the ensemble display.

If target-related and distractor-related biases contribute independently, then the Both Repeat condition should be equal the sum of the biases observed in the Target and the Distractor Repeat conditions.
In Experiment 1, the Both Repeat condition showed a super-additive pattern.
This pattern emerged at the two presentation times (200 ms and 500 ms).
However, at the shorter presentation time (150 ms) we did not observe a statistically significant super-additive pattern in the Both Repeat condition.
Although a weak numerical trend towards the super-additivity was visible, the effect could not reach significance.
However, the significance pattern should be treated with some care, since it is not always indicative of the difference in the magnitude of super-additivity for the two presentation times.

The occurrence of the combined effect of the target and the distractor templates is suggested by the numerical trend at the 150 ms, suggesting that the combined effect is already present at the shorter presentation times, and not only at longer ones.

The super-additive pattern may be explained by the fact that, when both the target and distractor colors were repeated, both feature representations for the target and distractor were re-activated concurrently in the same ensemble display.

The present results do not directly support this mechanism but may have been the case if target-related enhancement and distractor-related rejection had acted together to increase the bias, rather than each having an independent effect.
Finally, we examined the effects of the target and distractor templates on the variability of participants' responses.
Response variability was examined because attentional templates might affect not only the mean of the ensemble estimates, but also the precision of those estimates.

Attentional templates would change the contribution of the subsets, for instance: if one subset is prioritized over the other subset, prioritized subset may contribute more to the final ensemble orientation estimate.
This may influence the systematic bias and the uniformity of participants' responses between trials.
In both experiments, CSD is not significantly affected by the condition, although we observed systematic biases depending on the condition.
This suggests that attentional templates influenced ensemble estimates mostly via a shift in the direction of the bias and not via measurable changes in response precision.
Similar results were reported by Williams et al. (2021), noting that memory-matching biases impacted ensemble judgements without showing a significant influence of display type on CSD.
text.formatted: Similar results were reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Williams et al. (2021)</ref>, noting that memory-matching biases impacted ensemble judgements without showing a significant influence of display type on CSD.

text.text: These results indicate that ensemble estimates can be systematically altered by attentional prioritization without necessarily improving the response precision.
In Experiment 2, longer presentation time led lower response variability than shorter presentation time.

However, the level of template-based bias was not significantly altered with the length of the presentation. Tiurina et al. (2024) reported similar findings, showing that longer ensemble presentation times improved precision without changing the spatial weighting biases. Zepp and Dubé (2025) also showed that longer exposure times were associated with higher ensemble response precision.
text.formatted: However, the level of template-based bias was not significantly altered with the length of the presentation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Tiurina et al. (2024)</ref> reported similar findings, showing that longer ensemble presentation times improved precision without changing the spatial weighting biases. <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Zepp and Dubé (2025)</ref> also showed that longer exposure times were associated with higher ensemble response precision.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that attentional-template repetition and presentation duration affect different aspects of ensemble judgments: template repetition systematically biases orientation estimates without significantly affecting response variability, whereas longer presentation times improve response precision without significantly altering the bias.
In this study, templates were defined based on color.
However, in real-world scenarios, target and distractor templates can be defined by various other features, such as shape, size, orientation, or motion.
Our task required attentional selection guided by the color, and participants were expected to estimate average mean orientation of the lines.
This implies that such attentionbased prioritization on one feature dimension may affect ensemble judgements over another dimension.
Different features, however, may have different effectiveness in directing attention and in influencing later ensemble judgements.
Consequently, it is not known if the bias is a general property of attentional templates or if it is specific to color-based attentional selection.
This finding is consistent with the notion that template-based attentional weighting is applied across feature dimensions if similar biases were seen with templates defined by other features.
Instead, interdimensional differences might suggest attentional templates' effects vary with feature type for ensemble perception.
A related question that might be addressed in deeper research is whether templates based on other feature dimensions result in similar biases in the ensemble estimates.
Another limitation of this study is that we only compared the 150 ms and 500 ms presentation times.
The findings indicate that attentional templates influence ensemble perception; however, this design cannot determine at which cognitive stage the effect arises.

The present findings cannot determine whether attentional templates affect how the ensemble is encoded or whether they affect later processes, such as ensemble representation in working memory or the decision process involved in generating the response.
The bias observed at 150 ms does not prove that it arises during early perceptual processing but does show that it can appear in short presentation times.
Future studies might initially examine the time course of attentional template effect, by testing a wider range of presentation times.
Independent manipulation of encoding, retention, and response stages could then be employed to help to resolve the questions of when template-related biases occur.
To conclude, our results show that ensemble perception can be modulated by attentional templates, such that items do not necessarily contribute equally to the estimated average.
These templates were established during prior visual search.

Importantly, it was found that the bias produced by target-related templates was stronger than the bias produced by distractor-related templates, suggesting that these two types of attentional templates might differ in their effect on ensemble estimates.

These biases were already evident at short presentation times and did not increase with longer presentation times, showing that the influence of attentional templates was already present under brief presentation conditions.
Moreover, when both target and distractor templates were present, their combined influence could exceed the effects observed for the individual templates.
This finding suggests that target enhancement and distractor suppression may not operate independently but can jointly shape ensemble representations.

More broadly, our results indicate that the global impression we form of a visual scene is influenced not only by the information that is currently available but also by attentional templates carried over from preceding visual search.

The experimental design of Experiment 1.
Each trial started with a 500 ms fixation cross followed by 4-5 search displays.

Afterwards, the ensemble display appeared for 200 ms followed by an adjustment task which participants required to adjust the white line in the center of the display to match the average orientation of the entire ensemble from the previous display.
